## How Small Is a Small Sum of Squared Residuals?

Lecture 2.1 chose the line that makes the sum of squared residuals smaller than
any other line does, and on our 120 people that total is 2,692.8.

That number is in squared euro per hour, and it grows with the number of people
in the sample. It has no upper limit and no natural scale, so on its own it
ranks lines and nothing else.

Today builds the comparison it is missing: how much earnings vary in this sample
before schooling is mentioned at all.

::: {.defn title="Question"}
If I tell you the sum of squared residuals for a regression is 2,692.8, have I
told you anything about how well the line fits?
:::

## Lecture Plan

::: {.contributions}
1.  **Fitted Values and Residuals.** Splitting one person's earnings into the part the line gets and the part it misses.
2.  **Sums of Squares.** Adding those parts over 120 people, and deriving the identity that links the three totals.
3.  **What R-Squared Will Not Tell You.** Why a share of variation is not a verdict on a model or on a slope.
:::

# Fitted Values and Residuals

## Splitting One Person's Earnings Into Two Parts

The fitted line assigns every person a predicted wage, and whatever is left over
belongs to that person alone. Writing one person as the sum of the two is the
whole of this section [@wooldridge2020]:

```{=latex}
\begin{equation}
y_i = \hat{y}_i + \hat{u}_i
\qquad\text{where}\qquad
\hat{y}_i = \hat{\beta}_0 + \hat{\beta}_1 (x_i - 13)
\end{equation}
```

- $y_i$: what person $i$ actually earns per hour
- $\hat{y}_i$: the fitted value, what the line predicts for person $i$
- $\hat{u}_i$: the residual, the amount the line misses person $i$ by
- $\bar{y}$: the average of $y$ over the 120 people, 12.2490

::: {.caveat title="A Residual Is Not an Error"}
$u_i$ is the population error from 2.1, and we never see it. $\hat{u}_i$ is a
number we computed from the fitted line, so it inherits every flaw in that line.
If we had fitted a different line, every residual would be different while every
error stayed exactly as it was.
:::

## The Split Shown on One Person

```{=latex}
\fig{../_shared/figures/2-2_split.png}{One person's earnings split into a fitted value and a residual.}
```

::: {.tablenotes title="Three Heights, Two of Which We Choose"}
The dashed horizontal line is $\bar{y}$, at 12.2490. The solid line is the
fitted line from 2.1, slope 1.5227 and intercept 11.5680. Person $i$ sits above
both, and the distance from $\bar{y}$ up to that person is the sum of two
segments: $\bar{y}$ up to the line, and the line up to the person.
:::

## Three Facts About the Residuals, From Lecture 2.1

Least squares did not just pick a line. It picked the pair that makes these two
sums exactly zero, and every step today rests on them [@wooldridge2020]:

```{=latex}
\begin{equation}
\sum_{i=1}^{n} \hat{u}_i = 0
\qquad\qquad
\sum_{i=1}^{n} (x_i - 13)\, \hat{u}_i = 0
\end{equation}
```

The first says the residuals average to zero, so the fitted values average to
$\bar{y}$ as well. The second says the residuals retain no co-movement with
schooling. Together they put the point $(\bar{x}, \bar{y})$ on the fitted line.

::: {.takeaway title="These Two Sums Are the Only Inputs to Today's Derivation"}
Neither holds because of an assumption about the population. Both hold by
construction, for any sample of any 120 people, because the line was chosen to
make them hold.
:::

## A Large Residual Is Information About the Model

In 2.1 the largest residual was 17.23, and it supplied 296.9 of the total
2,692.8. It is tempting to read that person as an error in the data.

They are not. A residual is a statement about the pair, the person and the line,
and it cannot be assigned to one of them from its size alone. A person who earns
far more than thirteen years of schooling predicts may have a rare occupation, a
mistyped wage, or a feature the line was never given.

Lecture 4.1 is about reading residuals systematically: which patterns in them
indicate a fault in the specification rather than a fact about a person.

::: {.caveat title="The Residuals Sum to Zero Whatever Is Wrong With the Line"}
The two conditions above hold for a badly specified line exactly as they hold
for a well specified one. So no residual total can tell you the model is right,
and today's R-squared inherits that limitation in full.
:::

# Sums of Squares

## Three Totals, One for Each Kind of Variation

The per-person split becomes a comparison only once it is added over everybody.
Three totals do that, and each answers one question [@wooldridge2020]:

```{=latex}
\begin{equation}
\mathrm{TSS} = \sum_{i=1}^{n} (y_i - \bar{y})^2
\qquad
\mathrm{ESS} = \sum_{i=1}^{n} (\hat{y}_i - \bar{y})^2
\qquad
\mathrm{RSS} = \sum_{i=1}^{n} \hat{u}_i^{\,2}
\end{equation}
```

- $\mathrm{TSS}$: how much earnings vary, before schooling is mentioned
- $\mathrm{ESS}$: how much the fitted values vary around the same average
- $\mathrm{RSS}$: how much is left once the line has been subtracted

::: {.caveat title="Wooldridge Writes SST, SSE and SSR for These Three"}
The same three totals, different letters. Wooldridge notes that the first is
called SST or TSS with little confusion, but that SSE reads as "error sum of
squares" and is not: it is the explained total [@wooldridge2020]. Read the
letters in whichever book is open and match them to the formula, not the name.
:::

## The Total Sum of Squares as Vertical Segments

```{=latex}
\fig{../_shared/figures/2-2_tss.png}{Each segment runs from a person to the sample average of earnings.}
```

::: {.tablenotes title="The Benchmark Is the Average, Not the Line"}
This is the total we would face if we had never collected schooling: predict
12.2490 for everybody and square what is left. On our 120 people the segments
square and sum to 4,162.6. Every later total is measured against this one.
:::

## The Explained Sum of Squares as Vertical Segments

```{=latex}
\fig{../_shared/figures/2-2_ess.png}{Each segment now runs from the fitted line down to the sample average.}
```

::: {.tablenotes title="A Flat Line Would Contribute Nothing Here"}
These segments record how far the line departs from predicting the average for
everybody. If $\hat{\beta}_1$ were zero, every fitted value would equal 12.2490
and this total would be zero. On our 120 it is 1,469.8. The residual segments
are the ones drawn in 2.1, and they square and sum to 2,692.8.
:::

## Deriving the Identity: Splitting the Deviation From the Mean

Take one person's distance from the average and add and subtract the fitted
value, which splits it into the two segments on the last two exhibits:

```{=latex}
\begin{equation}
y_i - \bar{y} = \hat{u}_i + (\hat{y}_i - \bar{y})
\end{equation}
```

Square both sides and sum over the 120 people. The square of a sum is three
terms, and two of them are totals we have already named:

```{=latex}
\begin{equation}
\underbrace{\sum_{i=1}^{n} (y_i - \bar{y})^2}_{\mathrm{TSS}}
= \underbrace{\sum_{i=1}^{n} \hat{u}_i^{\,2}}_{\mathrm{RSS}}
+ \; 2\sum_{i=1}^{n} \hat{u}_i (\hat{y}_i - \bar{y})
+ \underbrace{\sum_{i=1}^{n} (\hat{y}_i - \bar{y})^2}_{\mathrm{ESS}}
\end{equation}
```

::: {.takeaway title="The Identity Holds Only If the Middle Term Is Zero"}
Nothing so far is special to least squares: this much is true of any line at
all. The whole argument reduces to one cross term, and the next frame is the
only place where the line being the least-squares line matters.
:::

## Deriving the Identity: Why the Cross Term Is Zero

Substitute the intercept 2.1 derived, $\hat{\beta}_0 = \bar{y} - \hat{\beta}_1
(\bar{x} - 13)$, into the fitted value. The centring constant cancels and what
remains is a deviation from the sample mean of schooling:

```{=latex}
\begin{equation}
\hat{y}_i - \bar{y}
= \hat{\beta}_0 + \hat{\beta}_1 (x_i - 13) - \bar{y}
= \hat{\beta}_1 (x_i - \bar{x})
\end{equation}
```

Put that into the cross term and take the constant $\hat{\beta}_1$ outside:

```{=latex}
\begin{equation}
\sum_{i=1}^{n} \hat{u}_i (\hat{y}_i - \bar{y})
= \hat{\beta}_1 \sum_{i=1}^{n} (x_i - \bar{x})\, \hat{u}_i
= \hat{\beta}_1 \Bigl[ \sum_{i=1}^{n} (x_i - 13)\, \hat{u}_i
  - (\bar{x} - 13) \sum_{i=1}^{n} \hat{u}_i \Bigr] = 0
\end{equation}
```

::: {.takeaway title="Both Bracketed Sums Are Conditions From Lecture 2.1"}
The first is zero because the residuals retain no co-movement with schooling.
The second is zero because the residuals sum to zero. Wooldridge reaches the
same step at eq (2.37) [@wooldridge2020]. R-squared behaves like a share only
because both of 2.1's conditions hold.
:::

## The Three Totals on Our 120 People

```{=latex}
\fig{../_shared/figures/2-2_bars.png}{The three totals as bars: the first is the height of the other two.}
```

::: {.tablenotes title="The Arithmetic Closes Exactly"}
$1{,}469.8 + 2{,}692.8 = 4{,}162.6$. The explained total and the residual total
add to the total variation with nothing left over, which is what the cross term
vanishing bought us. Most of the height of the first bar is residual.
:::

## Defining R-Squared From the Three Totals

The three totals are in squared euro per hour, so none of them can be compared
across datasets. Dividing one by another removes the units and the sample size
[@wooldridge2020]:

```{=latex}
\begin{equation}
R^2 = \frac{\mathrm{ESS}}{\mathrm{TSS}} = 1 - \frac{\mathrm{RSS}}{\mathrm{TSS}}
\end{equation}
```

- $R^2$: the share of the sample variation in earnings the line accounts for

::: {.defn title="R-Squared Is a Share Because the Identity Holds"}
The two expressions agree only because ESS and RSS add to TSS, and $R^2$ lies
between nought and one for the same reason. Without the cross term vanishing it
would be a ratio of two unrelated totals and could take any value at all.
:::

## R-Squared on Our 120 People

Both routes to the number use the totals from the bar chart, and they agree
because the identity holds:

```{=latex}
\begin{equation}
R^2 = \frac{1469.8}{4162.6} = 0.3531
\qquad\qquad
R^2 = 1 - \frac{2692.8}{4162.6} = 0.3531
\end{equation}
```

::: {.worked title="Reading the Number Out Loud"}
Schooling accounts for 35.31 per cent of the variation in hourly earnings across
these 120 people. The other 64.69 per cent is variation the line does not
reproduce. That sentence is about this sample and about the spread of earnings
in it, and it says nothing yet about whether 1.5227 is a good estimate.
:::

## R-Squared Is the Squared Correlation

Lecture 2.1 wrote the slope as a correlation times a ratio of standard
deviations, which is Wooldridge's second form of eq (2.19) [@wooldridge2020]:

```{=latex}
\begin{equation}
\hat{\beta}_1 = \hat{\rho}_{xy} \cdot \frac{\hat{\sigma}_y}{\hat{\sigma}_x}
\qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad
R^2 = \hat{\rho}_{xy}^{\,2}
\end{equation}
```

- $\hat{\rho}_{xy}$: the sample correlation between schooling and earnings, 0.5942
- $\hat{\sigma}_y, \hat{\sigma}_x$: the sample standard deviations of earnings and schooling

On our 120 people, $0.5942^2 = 0.3531$, which is the R-squared computed from the
totals. The appendix does the three lines of substitution.

::: {.takeaway title="In Simple Regression R-Squared Carries No New Information"}
With one regressor, R-squared is the correlation you already had, squared and
stripped of its sign. It cannot tell you the slope is positive, and it is the
same number whether earnings are regressed on schooling or schooling on
earnings. In multiple regression it stops being a correlation, which is where
its problems begin.
:::

## Adding a Variable That Cannot Matter

Two regressions on the same 120 people: earnings on schooling, and earnings on
schooling together with each person's height in centimetres.

::: {.defn title="Question"}
Which regression has the higher R-squared, and does your answer depend on
whether height has anything to do with earnings?
:::

# What R-Squared Will Not Tell You

## Adding Any Variable Raises the R-Squared

The height regression has the higher R-squared, and it does not depend on height
mattering. Least squares minimises RSS over a larger set of candidate lines, so
the new RSS cannot be larger than the old one. TSS is unchanged, since it never
involved a regressor. So $1 - \mathrm{RSS}/\mathrm{TSS}$ cannot fall.

A variable with no relation to earnings will still pick up some accidental
co-movement in 120 people, so in practice the R-squared rises rather than
staying still.

::: {.caveat title="R-Squared Cannot Compare Specifications"}
A criterion that never falls when a variable is added cannot choose between
specifications, because it ranks the largest model first every time. Lecture 3.1
introduces adjusted R-squared, which charges for each variable; Lecture 3.3 does
the comparison properly, with a test rather than a ranking.
:::

## A Straight Line Through a Curved Relationship

```{=latex}
\fig{../_shared/figures/2-2_rsq-curved.png}{Earnings rise and then fall, while the fitted straight line rises throughout.}
```

::: {.tablenotes title="The R-Squared Does Not Report the Curve"}
The straight line takes an average direction through a relation that reverses,
and returns a single positive slope and a respectable R-squared. Nothing in
either number records that the fit is wrong in shape. Lecture 3.2 fits the curve;
the residual plot in Lecture 4.1 is how you find out you need to.
:::

## A Low R-Squared Does Not Mean a Useless Slope

```{=latex}
\fig{../_shared/figures/2-2_rsq-loose.png}{A wide scatter around a clearly rising line: little of the spread accounted for.}
```

::: {.tablenotes title="Most of What Sets Earnings Is Not Schooling"}
Our own R-squared of 0.3531 says schooling leaves most of the spread in earnings
unaccounted for, which is a fact about how varied Irish earnings are and not a
fault in the line. Wooldridge's CEO salary regression returns 0.0132 on 209
firms, and he warns that a low R-squared does not make a regression useless
[@wooldridge2020].
:::

## Errors That Widen With Schooling Lower the R-Squared

Lecture 4.1 turns on heteroskedasticity: the errors stay centred on zero but
spread out more at higher levels of schooling, while the true slope stays at
1.30. The fitted slope barely shifts and the R-squared falls to under a third of
its value:

- baseline sample, errors of the same width at every schooling level: slope 1.5227, $R^2 = 0.3531$
- heteroskedastic sample, errors that fan out with schooling: slope 1.4784, $R^2 = 0.1014$

The slope answers "how much more does an extra year of schooling go with?" The
R-squared answers "how tightly do people cluster around that answer?" Widening
the errors at the top of the schooling range alters the second and leaves the
first where it is.

::: {.takeaway title="Two Different Questions, and Only One of Them Is About Size"}
R-squared has no units; the slope is in euro per hour per year of schooling.
No value of a unit-free share can tell you whether a euro figure is large enough
to matter, and Wooldridge notes that beginners weight R-squared far too heavily
in judging a regression [@wooldridge2020].
:::

## A High R-Squared Does Not Mean a Large Slope

```{=latex}
\fig{../_shared/figures/2-2_rsq-tight.png}{A tight scatter around a nearly flat line: almost all the spread accounted for.}
```

::: {.tablenotes title="The Slope Also Depends on the Two Standard Deviations"}
$\hat{\beta}_1 = \hat{\rho}_{xy} \cdot \hat{\sigma}_y / \hat{\sigma}_x$, and
R-squared fixes only the correlation. Holding the correlation at 0.99 and
shrinking $\hat{\sigma}_y$ shrinks the slope towards zero without touching the
R-squared. Any R-squared is compatible with any slope, in either direction.
:::

## Fit Measured Where the Line Was Chosen

R-squared is computed on the same 120 people the coefficients were chosen to
suit. Least squares picked the pair with the smallest possible RSS on those
rows, so it collected every accident in them that a line can collect.

On a fresh 120 from the same population those accidents are different ones, and
the line has no way to match them. Its RSS there will be larger, so the
R-squared will be lower. The drop is not a failure; it is the part of the
in-sample fit that was never about schooling.

::: {.caveat title="The Second 120 Were Set Aside Before Anything Was Fitted"}
Held out means held out. The moment a hold-out sample is used to choose a
specification it stops being one, because the chosen line has then been suited
to those rows too, and the honest comparison is gone.
:::

## R-Squared on the Hold-Out Sample

```{=latex}
\fig{../_shared/figures/2-2_fit-holdout.png}{The fitted line from our 120, drawn through 120 people it has never seen.}
```

::: {.tablenotes title="0.3531 In Sample, 0.2886 on the Hold-Out"}
The same line, the same population, the same slope of 1.5227: only the rows
differ. A fall of 0.0645, about a fifth of the in-sample figure, is the optimism
in fit measured on the data the line was chosen with. Report which of the two
numbers you are quoting.
:::

## What Would Have To Be True?

This time the question is asked of the sentence we read out loud, that schooling
accounts for 35.31 per cent of the variation in earnings in this sample.

::: {.defn title="Question"}
What would have to be true for this number to mean what we just said it means?
And what is the plausible story where it isn't?
:::

## Application

The app recomputes the three totals and the R-squared as you drag a single
person up or down, so you can watch the slope and the R-squared respond by
different amounts to the same movement.

::: {.defn title="Question"}
Before we fit anything: will the R-squared computed on the hold-out 120 come out
higher, lower, or about the same as the 0.3531 we got in sample?
:::

The lab for this lecture computes R-squared by hand from the three totals, then
checks it against `summary()`, and draws the residual plot.

## Summary: Residuals, Sums of Squares, and R-Squared

::: {.contributions}
1.  **Fitted Values and Residuals.** Every person splits into a fitted value and a residual, and the residuals sum to zero for any line least squares picks.
2.  **Sums of Squares.** TSS = ESS + RSS, because the cross term vanishes under the two conditions from 2.1: 1,469.8 + 2,692.8 = 4,162.6.
3.  **What R-Squared Will Not Tell You.** 0.3531 is a share of spread, not a verdict: it cannot rank specifications, and it fell to 0.2886 on the hold-out.
:::

## Next Lecture

Lecture 2.3 asks a different question about the same line: not how well it fits
these 120 people, but how far the slope lands from the 1.30 that generated them.

- **The Gauss-Markov Assumptions:** what must be true of the population first.
- **Unbiasedness:** the sense in which least squares gets the right answer.
- **Precision:** how far $\hat{\beta}_1$ would move if we drew another 120.

The residual sum of squares returns there in a new role: 2,692.8 is what the
standard error of the slope is built from.

## Derivation: R-Squared Is the Squared Correlation

The body frame asserts $R^2 = \hat{\rho}_{xy}^{\,2}$. Start from the fitted
deviation derived in the body, $\hat{y}_i - \bar{y} = \hat{\beta}_1
(x_i - \bar{x})$, so the explained total is the slope squared times the
schooling total:

```{=latex}
\begin{equation}
R^2 = \frac{\hat{\beta}_1^{\,2} \sum_{i=1}^{n}(x_i - \bar{x})^2}
           {\sum_{i=1}^{n}(y_i - \bar{y})^2}
    = \hat{\rho}_{xy}^{\,2}\,
      \frac{\hat{\sigma}_y^{\,2}}{\hat{\sigma}_x^{\,2}} \cdot
      \frac{\hat{\sigma}_x^{\,2}}{\hat{\sigma}_y^{\,2}}
    = \hat{\rho}_{xy}^{\,2}
\end{equation}
```

::: {.takeaway title="Dividing Both Totals by n Minus One Turns Them Into Variances"}
Substituting $\hat{\beta}_1 = \hat{\rho}_{xy}\hat{\sigma}_y/\hat{\sigma}_x$ from
p.26 gives the middle expression, and the two variance ratios cancel
[@wooldridge2020]. This is why R-squared carries no information beyond the
correlation when there is one regressor.
:::
